title: Active Passivation Tunes Hotspot Locations in GaN Transistors with In Situ Thermal Mechanical Visualization
authors: Yicheng Wei, Sihang Liu, Zimu Jiang, jinquan Zhang, Zifeng Huang, Han Yang, Yang He, Jin Wei, Zhe Cheng
abstract: Efficient thermal dissipation has become critical in emerging electronic devices. However, most existing studies have primarily focused on engineering heat dissipation pathways, largely overlooking the intrinsic behavior of the heat source itself. We demonstrate an active passivation technology that proactively tunes hotspot locations in GaN transistors. By adjusting the active passivation layer length, the hotspot is shifted from the gate edge to the drain-side AP edge, establishing a clear one-to-one spatial correlation. In-situ thermal-mechanical visualization via micro-Raman thermography, combined with multi-physics electro-thermal-mechanical simulations, directly captures the spatial redistribution of both temperature and thermal stress profiles. Electrical analysis confirms that this hotspot migration is driven by the spatial shift of the peak electric field and localized Joule heating. This proactive heat-source tuning strategy provides critical design guidelines for power electronics.
summary: This work demonstrates a novel technique using active passivation layers to proactively control where heat is generated within GaN transistors. By adjusting this layer, researchers can intentionally shift the hotspot away from critical areas like the gate edge towards the drain end. This approach offers crucial guidelines for designing high-power electronics by co-optimizing electric fields and thermal management.
main_problem: Localized Joule heating in GaN transistors operating at high power densities degrades performance by inducing thermal and mechanical stresses. Existing methods focus on external heat removal, ignoring the intrinsic behavior of the heat source.
main_result: Active passivation layers can proactively tune hotspot locations by shifting peak electric fields and localized Joule heating from the gate edge to the drain-side end of the active passivation layer.
method: The study combines in-situ micro-Raman thermography for experimental measurement with multi-physics electro-thermal-mechanical simulations (TCAD/FEA) for validation.
model_or_system: The physical system is a GaN High Electron Mobility Transistor (HEMT), comparing conventional structures to those enhanced with an Active Passivation layer. The analysis models the coupled electro-thermal-mechanical response under high bias conditions.
key_observables: Hotspot location, temperature rise ($\Delta T$), in-plane thermal stress profiles, peak electric field distribution, and device saturation current.
important_parameters: Active Passivation layer length (LAP), gate-drain distance (LGD), and applied bias/power density.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that manipulating the passivation structure can directly control the spatial redistribution of peak electric fields and subsequent heat generation, which is confirmed by simulation against experimental measurements.
figures_summary: Figures compare electrical properties, simulated electric field/Joule heating for conventional vs. active passivation devices; Figure 3 shows $\Delta T$ and stress maps comparing both structures; Figure 5 demonstrates the one-to-one correlation between LAP length and hotspot position.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of localized Joule heating, then introduces the AP structure to proactively tune hotspots. It presents electrical characterization, followed by in-situ thermal/mechanical visualization (Raman thermography), which is validated against coupled multi-physics simulations to confirm the hotspot migration mechanism.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state electronics, the core concept of using structural modification (passivation) to manage localized energy deposition and resulting stress fields has parallels in controlling energy flow or minimizing dissipation hotspots in quantum devices.
